newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - UK COMPOSITES.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - UK COMPOSITES.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN
Britain's composite insurers have in many ways had a good reporting season with profits, if anything, surprisingly on the upside.
But the results have told us little we didn't already know.
Claims experience has been good but markets remain tough with little evidence of rates turning.
Earlier comments that companies were putting through rises in private motor rates smack of talking the market up rather than a true reflection of industry conditions.

As one company chief executive said, while much reference has been made to increases in private motor rates, the point is that the buyer is continually being encouraged to seek lower alternative quotes, and in real terms increases achieved are marginal.
He doesn't see any significant upturn in the UK market until late 1998.
In many areas there are few signs of realistic underwriting disciplines re-emerging.

It is by no means certain that insurers can resist competing away excess capital but the signs are hopeful and a number of companies are reaffirming their commitment to letting business go rather than write at unprofitable levels.
The difficulty is that too much capacity is chasing the business.
New entrants are looking for market share by writing unprofitably while companies without the requisite skills are being tempted to write business which still makes technical profits for others.
The question of excess capital has yet to be suitably addressed.
The industry is averaging a solvency ratio - capital as a percentage of premium income - which tops 80 percent. Guardian Royal's has almost doubled to 95 percent since 1994.
Companies are understandably reluctant to take any major decisions on that front with stock markets - a major factor in the equation - at such strong levels.
They need capital to underwrite insurance. Premium income is invested, mostly in capital markets and insurers must take a view on how much capital is needed to meet future claims.
Return on capital is being eroded in some cases by the growing cash piles.

Guardian Royal and Royal & Sun head the list of those with excess capital burning holes in their pockets, but the latter has yet to complete the five percent buyback which it started after the full-year results.
Acquistions are becoming difficult with companies finding it hard to find things to buy at a reasonable price - particularly in the life sector.
Shareholders are likely to welcome having the cash handed back rather than overpaying for an acqusition or squandering capital by poor underwritng in highly competitive markets as in the past.
